newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian businessmen sober about '97 prospects.
newsitem.headline: Croatian businessmen sober about '97 prospects.

text.p: Croatian businessmen, buoyed by growth in 1996 after a five-year depression, expect the economy to expand in 1997 but have no high hopes for their own companies' prospects.

About 40 leading company and bank directors, surveyed by business weekly Privredni Vjesnik, said problems such as mounting inter-company debts and slow growth of export revenue might worsen before improving.
Croatia's industrial output rose three percent in 1996 and services such as tourism and transport also recovered, boosting gross domestic product (GDP) by well over five percent.

According to official and analysts' forecasts alike, this upward trend will solidify with even stronger growth rates next year. The government hopes for an almost 110 billion kuna ($20 billion) nominal GDP in 1997.

Many firms, including banks, shippers, seaside hotels, clothing and furniture manufacturers, see their profits rising or financial results at least consolidating after recent losses albeit through gigantic efforts.

But overall optimism based on a steady growth in domestic demand, which could prop up expansion of retail sales and other non-production branches, subsides in the face of concrete troubles lurking in the real sector.

A disparity between need and reality is best illustrated by fear expressed by companies that a lack of cash might restrain their investments in vital modernisation, while bankers reply that money is readily available for "sound projects."
Taught by experience, businessmen no longer look to the government for help beyond what it has pledged to do by overhauling key enterprises and the banking system.
Despite promising to gradually ease the fiscal burden by cutting taxes, it has dampened their hopes by raising the 1997 profit rate to 35 from 25 percent to boost budget revenue.
"All our efforts to improve agricultural production remain a desire, as there is no support to private initiative," said one disappointed head of a private farming concern.

A proposal to allow profits to be reinvested free of tax also fell flat, prompting criticism among entrepreneurs this would damage business as they struggle to strengthen their position in Croatia and win new markets.
Analysts warned the failure of the tax-free reinvestment proposal might also boomerang against the government if firms hid their profits or otherwise "licked off the cream".
Almost all exporters and particularly hoteliers on whose performance relies much of next year's growth, still wonder if they could not get the kind of support enjoyed by foreign competitors.
The oversized state-owned industry is languishing under a pile of old debts, only some of which have been taken over by government, and direly needs fresh capital injections.
Outright sell-off to foreign or capable Croatian investors, who could revamp the enterprises and win new business, seems an unlikely solution at least in the short run.
It is also shunned by the state because it could aggravate already high unemployment, now nearly 16 percent.

On the other hand, private companies are left to fend for themselves. Amid shrinking orders and thin backing from the country's banks, some of them just neglect to pay their current liabilities, from employment benefits to utility bills.
The new bankruptcy law, which comes into effect next year, is seen as offering inadequate protection to creditors, while possibly forcing potentially viable companies out of existence.

And with outdated production lines, capital cost of around 20 percent and high overheads, businessmen said Croatian goods might continue to lose battles against cheaper competition from other emerging-market countries, both in domestic and foreign markets.
